title: Chapter 19 — That Almost All The Americans Follow Industrial Callings
paragraphs: Of all the useful arts, agriculture is perhaps the one that improves most slowly among democratic nations. Often, indeed, it would seem to be stationary, because other arts are making rapid strides toward perfection. On the other hand, almost all the tastes and habits produced by equality of conditions naturally lead men to commercial and industrial occupations.

Suppose an active, enlightened, and free man, enjoying a competence but full of desires. He is too poor to live in idleness; he is rich enough to feel safe from the immediate fear of want, and he thinks about how he can better his condition. This man has acquired a taste for physical gratifications, in which thousands of his fellow men indulge around him. He has himself begun to enjoy these pleasures, and he is eager to increase his means of satisfying these tastes more completely. But life is slipping away, time is urgent—what is he to turn to? The cultivation of the ground promises an almost certain result from his efforts, but a slow one. Men are not enriched by it without patience and toil. Agriculture is therefore only suited to those who already have large, superfluous wealth, or to those whose poverty bids them only seek a bare subsistence. A man like the one we have imagined soon makes his choice: he sells his plot of ground, leaves his dwelling, and embarks on some hazardous but lucrative calling. Democratic communities abound in men of this kind, and in proportion as equality of conditions grows, their numbers increase. Thus democracy not only swells the number of working men, but it also leads men to prefer one kind of labor to another. While it diverts them from agriculture, it encourages their taste for commerce and manufactures. *a

[Footnote a: It has often been observed that manufacturers and merchants are inordinately given to physical gratifications, and this has been attributed to commerce and manufactures. But this, I think, is to take the effect for the cause. The taste for physical gratifications is not imparted to men by commerce or manufactures; rather, it is this taste that leads men to take up commerce and manufactures, as a means by which they hope to satisfy themselves more quickly and more completely. If commerce and manufactures increase the desire for well-being, it is because every passion gathers strength the more it is cultivated, and is increased by all the efforts made to satisfy it. All the causes that make the love of worldly welfare predominate in the human heart are favorable to the growth of commerce and manufactures. Equality of conditions is one of those causes; it encourages trade, not directly by giving men a taste for business, but indirectly by strengthening and expanding in their minds a taste for prosperity.]

This spirit can be seen even among the richest members of the community. In democratic countries, however opulent a man is supposed to be, he is almost always dissatisfied with his fortune, because he finds himself less rich than his father was, and he fears that his sons will be less rich than he is. Most rich men in democracies are therefore constantly haunted by the desire to acquire more wealth, and they naturally turn their attention to trade and manufactures, which seem to offer the readiest and most powerful means of success. In this respect they share the instincts of the poor, without feeling the same necessities. Or rather, they feel the most imperious necessity of all: that of not sinking in the world.

In aristocracies the rich are also those who govern. The attention they constantly devote to important public affairs diverts them from the smaller concerns that trade and manufactures demand. If the will of an individual should nevertheless turn his attention to business, the will of the body to which he belongs will immediately prevent him from pursuing it. For however much men may rail against the rule of numbers, they cannot wholly escape its sway. Even among those aristocratic bodies that most obstinately refuse to acknowledge the rights of the majority of the nation, a private majority is formed that governs the rest. *b

[Footnote b: Some aristocracies, however, have devoted themselves eagerly to commerce, and have cultivated manufactures with success. The history of the world could furnish several conspicuous examples. But generally speaking, it can be said that the aristocratic principle is not favorable to the growth of trade and manufactures. Moneyed aristocracies are the only exception to the rule. Among such aristocracies there are hardly any desires that do not require wealth to satisfy them; the love of riches becomes, so to speak, the main road of human passions, which is crossed by or connected with all lesser paths. The love of money and the thirst for that distinction which attaches to power are then so closely intermingled in the same souls that it becomes difficult to tell whether men grow greedy from ambition, or ambitious from greed. This is the case in England, where men seek to get rich in order to attain distinction, and seek distinctions as a manifestation of their wealth. The mind is then seized by both ends, and hurried into trade and manufactures, which are the shortest roads that lead to opulence.

This, however, strikes me as an exceptional and transitory state of affairs. When wealth has become the only symbol of aristocracy, it is very difficult for the wealthy to keep sole possession of political power, to the exclusion of all other men. The aristocracy of birth and pure democracy are at the two extremes of the social and political state of nations: between them the moneyed aristocracy finds its place. It approaches the aristocracy of birth by conferring great privileges on a small number of persons; it belongs to the democratic element insofar as these privileges may in turn be acquired by all. It often forms a natural transition between these two conditions of society, and it is hard to say whether it closes the reign of aristocratic institutions or already opens the new era of democracy.]

In democratic countries, where money does not bring those who possess it political power, but often removes them from it, the rich do not know how to spend their leisure. They are driven into active life by the restlessness and greatness of their desires, by the extent of their resources, and by the taste for what is extraordinary that is almost always felt by those who rise, by whatever means, above the crowd. Trade is the only road open to them. In democracies nothing is greater or more brilliant than commerce: it attracts the attention of the public and fills the imagination of the multitude; all the energetic passions are directed toward it. Neither their own prejudices nor those of anyone else can prevent the rich from devoting themselves to it. The wealthy members of democracies never form a body that has manners and regulations of its own; the opinions peculiar to their class do not hold them back, and the common opinions of their country urge them on. Moreover, since all the large fortunes to be found in a democratic community have come from commerce, many generations must pass before those who possess them can have entirely laid aside their habits of business.

Confined within the narrow space that politics leaves them, rich men in democracies eagerly throw themselves into commercial enterprise. There they can extend and employ their natural advantages. Indeed, it is even by the boldness and scale of their industrial speculations that we can measure how little esteem they would have shown for productive industry had they been born into an aristocracy.

A similar observation also applies to all men living in democracies, whether poor or rich. Those who live in the midst of democratic fluctuations always have before their eyes the phantom of chance, and they end by liking all undertakings in which chance plays a part. They are therefore all led to engage in commerce, not only for the sake of the profit it holds out to them, but for the love of the constant excitement that pursuit produces.

The United States of America have only been free for half a century [in 1840] from the state of colonial dependence in which they stood toward Great Britain. The number of large fortunes there is small, and capital is still scarce. Yet no people in the world has made such rapid progress in trade and manufactures as the Americans. They are today the second maritime nation in the world, and although their manufactures have to struggle with almost insurmountable natural obstacles, they are not prevented from making great and daily advances. In the United States the greatest undertakings and speculations are carried out without difficulty, because the whole population is engaged in productive industry, and because the poorest as well as the most opulent members of the commonwealth are ready to combine their efforts for these purposes. The result is that a stranger is constantly amazed by the immense public works carried out by a nation that contains, so to speak, no rich men. The Americans arrived only yesterday on the territory they inhabit, and they have already changed the whole order of nature to their own advantage. They have joined the Hudson to the Mississippi, and made the Atlantic Ocean communicate with the Gulf of Mexico, across a continent more than five hundred leagues wide that separates the two seas. The longest railroads built up to the present time are in America. But what most astonishes me in the United States is not so much the marvelous grandeur of some undertakings as the countless multitude of small ones. Almost all the farmers of the United States combine some trade with agriculture; most of them make agriculture itself a trade. It seldom happens that an American farmer settles for good on the land he occupies. Especially in the districts of the Far West, he brings land into cultivation in order to sell it again, not to farm it. He builds a farmhouse on the speculation that, since the state of the country will soon be changed by the increase of population, a good price will be obtained for it. Every year a swarm of inhabitants from the North arrive in the Southern States and settle in the areas where the cotton plant and the sugar cane grow. These men cultivate the soil in order to make it produce in a few years enough to enrich them; and they already look forward to the time when they may return home to enjoy the competence thus acquired. Thus the Americans carry their business-like qualities into agriculture, and their trading passions are displayed there as in their other pursuits.

The Americans make immense progress in productive industry, because they all devote themselves to it at once; and for this same reason they are exposed to very unexpected and formidable troubles. Since they are all engaged in commerce, their commercial affairs are affected by such various and complex causes that it is impossible to foresee what difficulties may arise. Since they are all more or less engaged in productive industry, at the slightest shock given to business all private fortunes are put in jeopardy at the same time, and the State is shaken. I believe that the recurrence of these commercial panics is an endemic disease of the democratic nations of our age. It can be made less dangerous, but it cannot be cured, because it does not come from accidental circumstances, but from the temperament of these nations.
